strengths: The authors introduce the DDPP framework for steering MNDMs by treating the task as sampling from a Bayesian posterior, which is an innovative approach for discrete generative models. They derive three scalable, simulation-free objectives that make fine-tuning computationally efficient, even for large pre-trained models.

Extensive experiments were conducted across diverse tasks, including image modeling, text generation, and protein sequence design. DDPP demonstrated strong performance across all domains, highlighting its adaptability to various data types and applications.

The paper includes wet-lab validation for protein sequence tasks, confirming the practical applicability of the model in real-world protein design. This physical validation of AI-generated outputs adds quite a lot credibility.
The paper is clearly written and well-structured. The presentation is overall good.
The paper provides a nice overview of the problem of discrete guidance and several sensible solutions to it.
Implemented several variants and compared them to each other, offering more signal to the community about promising directions.

The significance of the work is substantial because discrete diffusion models are increasingly popular in both text applications, where guidance can equate to controllability/alignment, and for scientific modalities, where guidance is used for solving inverse problems.
While the originality is not high, the quality of the work's presentation and analysis compensates for it.
Evaluation of the method is mostly satisfactory, spanning multiple modalities and including wet lab experiments.
Addresses the important problem of controlled generation, which has significant applications as discussed in the paper.
Proposed DDPP framework (three versions) is a novel approach that efficiently tackles the problem without simulating the reverse diffusion process.

Empirical results demonstrate the superiority of the DDPP method over several baseline methods, including best-of-N, SVDD, and RTB, highlighting the effectiveness and potential of the proposed framework in the context of discrete diffusion models.
The paper is well-written and clearly organized, providing sufficient details to understand and replicate the experiments.
The paper presents DDPP, a method to align Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) with reward functions directly at inference, skipping RL and costly sampling typical for autoregressive models.

DDPP is backed by theories, and its three variants—DDPP-IS, DDPP-LB, and DDPP-KL—are designed for both differentiable and non-differentiable rewards, enabling efficient MDM fine-tuning with strong performance across tasks.
The writing flow of this work is clear, with a smooth and easy to follow presentation.
weaknesses: Including autoregressive models as baselines could be useful, as they are widely used and effective in many generative tasks. Specifically, comparing against fine-tuned autoregressive models, which are often optimized for similar objectives, would provide a more comprehensive understanding of DDPP's performance.

Since DDPP-IS involves MCMC, it would be helpful to analyze the computational cost of each method, covering both training and inference phases, including a breakdown of time complexity, number of forward passes, reward function evaluations, and MCMC overhead.
The paper does not make any foundational contributions that are broadly applicable beyond guidance of discrete diffusion models, nor does it present observations that are deeply surprising.

The contributions are driven by a narrow practical goal of approximating log Z (or foregoing its approximation) when training a secondary model q to approximate the transition distribution, which may limit broader impact.

Evaluation results are fairly reasonable with some baseline comparisons, but wet lab experiments are hard to interpret because only non-control methods are DDPP, making it unclear how much posterior inference contributes versus other sampling or filtering facets.
Requires training a secondary model; if inference is limited, the training cost may not be justified, as inference throughput is often more important than latency.
Best-of-N sampling performs well for relatively small N, sometimes approaching DDPP performance, and can be deployed out of the box with only minor inference overhead.
The methodologies introduced in the paper are somewhat confusing, and the underlying intuition behind their design is not fully grasped.
The writing of the paper, particularly the mathematical explanations, could benefit from improvement.
The theoretical parts are not very easy to follow; simplifying theory sections and providing illustrations would improve readability, and motivations/differences for the three variants are unclear.
It remains unclear if DDPP can generalize to other types of discrete diffusion models or if the results depend heavily on the MDM-specific setup.
Limited discussion of computational costs relative to baseline approaches; assuming SVDD is computationally friendly, DDPP may not be superior in computation efficiency.

The novelty is questionable as the algorithm appears to be a variance of path consistency learning in the discrete setting, making it unclear why this algorithm is special compared to the standard continuous setting and what technical difficulty the extension entails.

Experimental part is incomplete; lacking baselines such as classifier-free guidance, DDPO/DPOK, direct reward backpropagation, and classifier guidance in discrete diffusion, as well as comparisons with sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods.

Discussion of SVDD performance is incomplete; SVDD is basically a nested-SMC whose performance depends heavily on the duplication number, yet the paper lacks detailed analysis of this dependency, weakening empirical evaluation.

Claim that certain rewards used in experiments are not differentiable is imprecise; many protein forward/inverse folding models, including AlphaFold, are differentiable, raising questions why such differentiable rewards were not incorporated.
